There is no closed form for this one, so it is simulated: two hundred thousand independent runs of two hundred trades each, outcomes drawn at a 45% win rate, seed 20260901. The figures below are the distribution of the worst peak-to-trough drawdown in each run, and the last two columns are what an account risking a fixed fraction of its current equity actually lost across that same stretch of trades. Every outcome here is +2R or −1R, so the equity is a whole number at every step and the drawdown is too; re-running under other seeds returns the same integers, give or take one at the far tail.

The last two columns are where sizing stops being theoretical, and they are worth reading across rather than down. Nothing differs between them except the fraction of the account you put behind each trade. Same method, same edge, same trades in the same order: one trader is down 15% in the one-in-twenty year and recovers, the other is down 39% and needs to make 65% to get back to level. Neither figure is the drawdown compounded as a run of losses, which understates both, because a 16R fall is a longer stretch than sixteen trades and contains winners as well. Lesson 20 is where that decision gets made properly, and where the gap between those two arithmetics turns out to matter; the point here is only that the depth of a normal bad run is a number you choose, and the frequency of one is not.
